name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q01 - Longitudinal section of mitochondrion structure

questiontext.text: In the given longitudinal section of a mitochondrion, which labelled part represents the infoldings of the inner membrane that increase the surface area?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a longitudinal section of a mitochondrion with four labelled regions: P points to the outermost smooth boundary, Q points to the space between the outer and inner membranes, R points to the dense homogeneous inner compartment, and S points to an inward fold of the inner membrane projecting into the inner compartment.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A standard longitudinal schematic of a eukaryotic mitochondrion is interpreted, where the two concentric membranes divide the organelle into an outer aqueous compartment and an inner aqueous compartment.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Mitochondria are double-membrane-bound organelles. The outer membrane forms a continuous limiting boundary, while the inner membrane forms infoldings called cristae towards the matrix to increase the surface area for enzymes associated with aerobic respiration.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Matching each label to the mitochondrial structure: P corresponds to the outer membrane; Q corresponds to the inter-membrane space (outer compartment); R corresponds to the matrix (inner compartment); and S corresponds to a crista, which is an infolding of the inner membrane.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The inward folds that increase surface area are specifically the cristae. Therefore, the labelled part S represents the crista.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q02 - Fluid mosaic model of plasma membrane

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram illustrates the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane with four labelled parts: P indicates the phospholipid bilayer, Q indicates a protein resting on the outer surface of the bilayer, R indicates a protein spanning through the bilayer, and S indicates a branched sugar chain attached to the spanning protein.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The Singer and Nicolson (1972) fluid mosaic model is used, where lipids form a quasi-fluid bilayer and membrane proteins are classified as peripheral or integral depending on ease of extraction.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In the phospholipid bilayer, polar hydrophilic heads face the outer aqueous sides while nonpolar hydrophobic tails face the inner core. Peripheral proteins lie on the membrane surface, whereas integral proteins are partially or totally buried in the membrane.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Evaluating each labelled structure: P (phospholipid bilayer) has polar heads facing outward and nonpolar tails facing inward, not the reverse. Q is a peripheral protein lying on the surface, not buried in the hydrophobic core. R is an integral protein buried across the membrane bilayer, making it difficult to extract. S is a sugar (carbohydrate) chain attached to the integral protein, not cholesterol.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The only biologically accurate statement is that component R (the integral protein) is partially or totally buried in the membrane and cannot be easily extracted.

answer.text: Component P consists of polar tails facing inward and nonpolar heads facing outward.
Component Q is completely buried inside the hydrophobic core of the lipid bilayer.
Component R is partially or totally buried in the membrane and cannot be easily extracted.
Component S represents cholesterol, which provides rigidity to the membrane.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q03 - Classification of chromosomes by centromere

questiontext.text: Identify the types of chromosomes labelled W, X, Y, and Z based on the position of the centromere in the given diagram.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram displays four chromosomes labelled W, X, Y, and Z, each consisting of two chromatids held together by a centromere at different positions along the chromosome length.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Chromosomes are classified into four standard morphological types based strictly on the relative position of the primary constriction (centromere) and the resulting arm lengths.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. A metacentric chromosome has a middle centromere forming two equal arms.
2. A sub-metacentric chromosome has a centromere slightly away from the middle, forming one shorter arm and one longer arm.
3. An acrocentric chromosome has a centromere situated close to its end, forming one extremely short arm and one very long arm.
4. A telocentric chromosome has a terminal centromere.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In W, the centromere is exactly in the middle, producing two equal arms, so W is metacentric. In X, the centromere is slightly off-centre, producing one shorter and one longer arm, so X is sub-metacentric. In Y, the centromere is close to one end, producing an extremely short arm and a very long arm, so Y is acrocentric. In Z, the centromere is at the terminal end, so Z is telocentric.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct sequence from left to right is: W is metacentric, X is sub-metacentric, Y is acrocentric, and Z is telocentric.

answer.text: W: Metacentric, X: Sub-metacentric, Y: Acrocentric, Z: Telocentric
W: Sub-metacentric, X: Metacentric, Y: Telocentric, Z: Acrocentric
W: Metacentric, X: Acrocentric, Y: Sub-metacentric, Z: Telocentric
W: Telocentric, X: Acrocentric, Y: Sub-metacentric, Z: Metacentric

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q04 - Transverse section of eukaryotic axoneme

questiontext.text: The given diagram represents the transverse section of the axoneme of a eukaryotic cilium or flagellum. Which of the following correctly identifies the labelled structures P, Q, R, and S?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a transverse section of a eukaryotic cilium or flagellum core (axoneme) with four labelled features: P points to the outer limiting membrane, Q points to one of the nine paired peripheral microtubule rings, R points to the red ring enclosing the central pair of microtubules, and S points to a spoke connecting a peripheral doublet to the central ring.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The standard ultrastructure of a eukaryotic cilium or flagellum as revealed by electron microscopy follows the 9+2 axonemal organisation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Eukaryotic cilia and flagella are covered with the plasma membrane. Their axoneme contains nine doublets of radially arranged peripheral microtubules and a pair of centrally located microtubules (9+2 array). The central tubules are connected by bridges and enclosed by a central sheath, which is connected to one tubule of each peripheral doublet by a radial spoke (nine radial spokes in total).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Identifying each label: P is the plasma membrane covering the cilium/flagellum; Q is one of the nine peripheral microtubule doublets (unlike centrioles which have triplets); R is the central sheath enclosing the two central microtubules; and S is a radial spoke linking the peripheral doublet to the central sheath.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Matching all four structures simultaneously gives: P as the plasma membrane, Q as the nine peripheral microtubule doublets, R as the central sheath, and S as the radial spoke.

answer.text: P: Cell wall; Q: Nine peripheral triplets; R: Hub; S: Interdoublet bridge
P: Plasma membrane; Q: Nine peripheral singlets; R: Central sheath; S: Central microtubule
P: Nuclear envelope; Q: Nine peripheral doublets; R: Central sheath; S: Radial spoke
P: Plasma membrane; Q: Nine peripheral microtubule doublets; R: Central sheath; S: Radial spoke
